chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding a place to live

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your housing options and where to start
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use 211 and reentry programs to list three housing options you can apply for.
This lesson builds toward: Using 211 and reentry programs, you will list housing options you can apply for, with phone number, cost, rules and what to bring for each.
Most people coming home move through more than one kind of housing: staying with family, a shelter, transitional or reentry housing, sober living, renting a room, and later an apartment of their own. Each step is fine. The goal is a safe place now and a better place next.
211 is the easiest place to start. You can call 211 or go to 211.org to reach a local helper who connects you with housing, food, utility help, health care and more. Calls are confidential. Tell them you are coming home from prison or jail and ask about reentry housing.
Public housing and Housing Choice Vouchers (often called Section 8) are run by your local Public Housing Agency (PHA). Waiting lists can be long or closed, so get on them early and keep your contact details up to date.
If you are on parole or probation, your officer may need to approve where you live. Ask before you sign anything.
Step by step:
- Call 211 or visit 211.org and ask about reentry and transitional housing.
- Ask a reentry program or your parole or probation officer for housing lists.
- Find your local Public Housing Agency and ask how to join its waiting lists.
- Write down three options: name, phone, cost, rules and what to bring.
- Check with your officer that the address is allowed.
Words to know:
- 211: a free, confidential phone and web service that connects you to local help.
- Transitional housing: short-term housing with support, often for people coming home.
- Public Housing Agency (PHA): the local office that runs public housing and housing vouchers.
- Housing Choice Voucher: help paying rent to a private landlord, often called Section 8.
Official sources:
- 211: Find local help
- HUD: Public housing program
Try it now: Call 211 or visit 211.org and ask for reentry or transitional housing near you. Write down three options with the phone number, cost, rules and what each asks you to bring.
You can now use 211 and your local Public Housing Agency to find housing options and list what each one needs.

options: A hotel you pay by the night
Short-term housing with support, often for people coming home
A house you buy
A shelter that only opens in winter
check.why: Transitional housing is short-term housing with support while you get settled.

check.q: You are on parole and a friend offers you a room. What would you do before moving in?
options: Move in tonight
Sign a lease right away
Check that your officer approves the address
Tell no one
check.why: Parole conditions may limit where you can live, so you check first.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Applying for housing with a record
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain what housing rules say about records and how to ask for a fair look at your application.
This lesson builds toward: Given a housing provider and the rules about records, you will explain what the rules say about records and ask for a fair look at your application, asking whether there is a written policy and whether you can give proof of rehabilitation.
Federal rules require public housing agencies to deny a few groups: anyone who must register as a sex offender for life; anyone ever convicted of making methamphetamine on federally assisted housing property; and, for three years, a household evicted from federally assisted housing for drug activity, unless the person finished an approved rehab program or the situation has changed. They can also deny current illegal drug use.
For most other records, the housing agency decides using its own written policy. Before it denies you because of a criminal record, it must tell you and give you a copy of the record and a chance to dispute it. It may not charge you for the records check. Ask for its policy, and ask for a review if you are denied.
Private landlords can usually look at criminal history. A record is not a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act, and HUD has said it is ending earlier federal guidance that limited background checks. State and city laws may protect you more. In California, landlords cannot use arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records or juvenile records, cannot ban everyone with a record, and must show a conviction is directly related to being a good tenant.
If you think a landlord in California broke these rules, you can contact the California Civil Rights Department, generally within one year. In other states, ask legal aid or your state's civil rights office.
Step by step:
- Ask each housing provider for its written policy on criminal records.
- Read your own record first so nothing surprises you.
- Bring proof of rehabilitation to the application.
- If denied, ask in writing for the reason, a copy of the record used and a review.
- If you think the law was broken, contact legal aid or your state civil rights office.
Words to know:
- Fair Housing Act: the federal law against housing discrimination based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, family status or disability.
- Protected class: a group the law protects from discrimination.
- Federally assisted housing: housing paid for in part by federal programs, like public housing.
- Informal review: a meeting to ask a housing agency to look again at a denial.
Official sources:
- 24 CFR 960.204: Denial of admission for criminal activity or drug abuse (Cornell LII)
- HUD: Fair Housing Act overview
- California Civil Rights Department: Housing
Try it now: Call or visit the website of one housing provider from your list and ask: Do you have a written policy on criminal records? Can I give you proof of rehabilitation with my application? Write down the answers.
You can now explain the main housing rules about records, ask a provider for its policy, and ask for a review if you are denied.

check.q: Who runs public housing and Housing Choice Vouchers in your area?
options: The local Public Housing Agency
The police department
Your parole officer
The IRS
check.why: Your local Public Housing Agency runs these programs and sets its own policy.

check.q: You want to apply to a housing provider but worry about your record. What would you do?
options: Leave the record off and hope
Give up and not apply
Pay extra to skip the check
Ask for their written policy and whether you can add proof of rehabilitation
check.why: Asking about the policy and offering proof helps get a fair look.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building a rental packet
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put together a rental packet that answers a landlord's worries before they ask.
This lesson builds toward: Given the papers you have, you will put together a rental packet and spot rental scams, with a papers checklist and a short letter about what you have done since, and no payment before seeing a place.
A landlord wants to know three things: will you pay on time, will you take care of the place, and will you get along with neighbors. A rental packet answers all three in one folder.
Include: a photo ID; proof of income such as pay stubs, an offer letter or a benefits letter; references from an employer, case manager, program staff or faith leader; certificates from programs you finished; and a short letter about your record that says what happened, what you have done since, and why you will be a good tenant.
Watch for rental scams. Never send money by wire, gift card or payment app before you have seen the place in person and signed a lease. Be careful with any deal that seems too cheap or rushes you.
Know what you can pay. Many programs use a rule of thumb that rent should be about a third of your income or less. Ask about all move-in costs: deposit, first month and application fees.
Step by step:
- Get a folder and make copies of your ID and proof of income.
- Ask two or three people for reference letters.
- Add certificates from programs you finished.
- Write a short letter about your record, ending with why you will be a good tenant.
- Before paying anything, see the place in person and get a written lease.
Words to know:
- Rental packet: a folder of papers that shows a landlord you are a good tenant.
- Reference: a person who can speak well about you.
- Security deposit: money you pay before moving in that the landlord holds in case of damage.
- Lease: the written rental agreement.
Try it now: Start your rental packet. Make a checklist of the papers you have and the ones you still need. Write the first draft of your short letter: one sentence about what happened, two about what you have done since, and one about why you will be a good tenant.
You can now build a rental packet that shows a landlord you will pay, take care of the place and be a good neighbor, and spot rental scams.

check.q: Which belongs in a rental packet?
options: Proof of income and reference letters
Your full case file
Your bank password
A copy of your Social Security card for anyone
check.why: Income proof and references answer a landlord's main worries.

check.q: A landlord wants a deposit by wire transfer before you see the apartment. What would you do?
options: Send it quickly before someone else does
Send half
Refuse and look for another place
Send it by gift card instead
check.why: Asking for payment before you see the place is a scam warning sign.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: American Job Centers and reentry job programs
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find your nearest American Job Center and a reentry job program and know what to ask them.
This lesson builds toward: Using CareerOneStop or 211, you will find your nearest American Job Center and second-chance job leads, with address, phone, hours and questions to ask on your first visit.
American Job Centers are public job offices found across the country. They help with job searches, résumés, training, and sometimes paid training or help with work clothes and tools. You can find the nearest one on CareerOneStop (careeronestop.org), a website from the US Department of Labor, or by calling 211.
The Department of Labor also funds reentry employment programs for formerly incarcerated adults and young people. Reentry organizations, community colleges and some unions run job training and apprenticeships too.
When you visit, ask: What training is free for me? Do you work with employers who hire people with records? Can you help me with a bonding letter or the Work Opportunity Tax Credit paperwork? Can you help with work clothes, tools or a bus pass?
Step by step:
- Go to careeronestop.org and search for an American Job Center near you, or call 211.
- Ask a reentry program which job programs it works with.
- Bring your ID, any résumé you have, and certificates.
- Ask the four questions in this lesson and write down the answers.
- Set a date for your next visit.
Words to know:
- American Job Center: a free public office that helps people find jobs and training.
- CareerOneStop: a US Department of Labor website for jobs, training and finding job centers.
- Apprenticeship: a paid job where you learn a trade while you work.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop: Find American Job Centers
- US Department of Labor: Reentry employment
Try it now: Find your nearest American Job Center. Write down its address, phone number and hours, and the four questions you will ask on your first visit.
You can now find an American Job Center and a reentry job program and ask them for the help you need.

check.q: What does an American Job Center offer?
options: Paid jobs only at the center
Free help with job searches, résumés and training
Housing vouchers
Loans for cars
check.why: American Job Centers give free job search, résumé and training help.

check.q: You are at a job center for the first time. Which question would you ask?
options: Can you write my record off?
How much do you charge?
Can I skip the application?
Which employers here hire people with records?
check.why: Job center staff often know local second-chance employers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Second-chance employers, WOTC and federal bonding
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain to an employer how the Work Opportunity Tax Credit and the Federal Bonding Program can help them hire you.
This lesson builds toward: Given the Work Opportunity Tax Credit and the Federal Bonding Program, you will explain to an employer how they can help them hire you, in a two-sentence pitch, checked against irs.gov for whether WOTC is in effect.
A second-chance employer is a business that is open to hiring people with records. Look for them through job centers, reentry programs, staffing agencies that work with reentry, trade unions, and job posts that say fair chance or second chance.
The Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) is a federal tax credit for employers, not money paid to you. One group it covers is qualified ex-felons: people hired within a year of a felony conviction or release from prison. The employer and you fill out IRS Form 8850 on or before the day of the job offer, and the employer sends it to the state within 28 days after you start. The IRS page said the credit covered people who started work by 31 December 2025. Check irs.gov to see whether it has been renewed before you mention it.
The Federal Bonding Program gives employers a free fidelity bond, a kind of insurance against employee theft, for the first six months of a job. Each bond covers up to $5,000 with no deductible, and there are no forms for you to fill out. People with records are one of the groups it serves. Your state bonding coordinator, listed on bonds4jobs.com, arranges it.
Many employers have never heard of these programs. Telling them shows you have done your homework and lowers their risk.
Step by step:
- Make a list of second-chance employers from job centers, reentry programs and job posts.
- Check irs.gov to see whether WOTC is in effect now.
- Find your state bonding coordinator on bonds4jobs.com.
- Practice a two-sentence pitch about WOTC and bonding.
- Bring the Form 8850 and bonding information to interviews.
Words to know:
- Second-chance employer: a business that is open to hiring people with records.
- Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC): a federal tax credit for employers who hire people from certain groups.
- Fidelity bond: insurance that protects an employer against loss from employee theft.
- Form 8850: the IRS form used to start the WOTC process.
Official sources:
- IRS: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
- US Department of Labor: Work Opportunity Tax Credit
- Federal Bonding Program: About
Try it now: Write your two-sentence employer pitch. For example: If you hire me, you may be able to claim the Work Opportunity Tax Credit. I can also come with a free Federal Bonding Program bond that covers my first six months. Then find your state bonding coordinator on bonds4jobs.com.
You can now find second-chance employers and explain WOTC and federal bonding to an employer in plain words.

check.q: Who receives the Work Opportunity Tax Credit?
options: The worker
The parole office
The employer
The job center
check.why: WOTC is a tax credit the employer may claim for hiring you.

check.q: You plan to tell an employer about WOTC in an interview. What would you do first?
options: Check irs.gov to see whether it is in effect now
Promise them a set dollar amount
Ask AI to fill in Form 8850 with your details
Skip it because employers never care
check.why: WOTC rules can change, so you check irs.gov before mentioning it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Applying and answering questions about your record
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Apply to a second-chance job and answer questions about your record with confidence.
This lesson builds toward: Given a question about your record in an interview, you will answer it briefly and honestly, saying what happened, what you have done since and why you are ready, with no case numbers typed into AI.
Apply to several jobs each week. Keep a simple list with the employer, the job, the date you applied and what happens next. Follow up after about a week if you have not heard back.
Many states and cities have fair-chance or ban-the-box laws that delay record questions until later in hiring. Learn your local rule. When the question comes, be honest. Lying about a record is a common reason to lose a job later.
Answer in three short parts: what happened, in one sentence and without excuses; what you have done since, such as programs, work, school and staying on track; and why you are ready for this job. Then move back to your skills. Practice it out loud until it feels calm.
Bring proof: certificates, a reference letter, and your WOTC and bonding information. An AI assistant can help you practice interview questions, but never type your case numbers or other private details into it.
Step by step:
- Apply to several jobs each week and track them in a list.
- Learn your state or city fair-chance rule.
- Write your three-part answer about your record.
- Practice it out loud with a person or an AI assistant, without private details.
- Bring certificates, references, and WOTC and bonding information to the interview.
Words to know:
- Follow up: contacting an employer again to check on your application.
- Fair-chance law: a law that limits when employers can ask about a record.
- Reference letter: a letter from someone who can speak well about your work or character.
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page housing-and-jobs plan with two housing options, your rental packet checklist, your nearest American Job Center, three second-chance employers or job leads, and your two-sentence WOTC and bonding pitch. Then say your three-part answer about your record out loud once.
You can now apply to second-chance jobs, track your applications, and answer questions about your record honestly and calmly.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Housing options Fewer than two options, or missing contact details. Two housing options with contact details and what to bring. Also notes cost and rules, and that the address was checked with parole if needed. Rental packet checklist No checklist. A checklist of papers you have and papers you still need. Includes a first draft of the short letter about what you have done since. Job help and leads No job center or fewer than three leads. Nearest American Job Center and three second-chance employers or job leads. Includes the questions you will ask on your first visit. Employer pitch No pitch, or it promises a set dollar amount. A two-sentence pitch about WOTC and the Federal Bonding Program. Also names the state bonding coordinator and notes WOTC was checked on irs.gov. Answer about your record Not practiced, or long, blaming or untrue. Said out loud once: what happened, what you have done since, why you are ready. Short, calm and practiced more than once. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What are the three parts of a good answer about your record?
options: Your case number, your sentence and your release date
What happened, what you have done since and why you are ready
Who was to blame, how unfair it was and how long ago
Nothing, because you should not answer
check.why: A brief, honest three-part answer shows growth and readiness.

check.q: You want AI to help you practice interview answers. What would you do?
options: Type your case numbers so it knows your history
Paste your full record into it
Use general words and keep case numbers out
Ask it to invent a clean record
check.why: You can practice with AI without sharing private case details.
